content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a double knowledge distillation for multi-agent continual learning in both output and latent space without access to previous data. The authors consider two scenarios, especially for the case of sequential and independent initialization settings. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**:


* The problem of multi-agent continual learning is interesting


**Weakness**:


* The proposed methods have limited novelty, the method simply combines two kinds of knowledge distillation in the model output and in latent space. Also, adopt some methods by sampling data from external resources, which are common procedures in existing works. 


* What is the memory cost for the proposed methods, especially compared to traditional and simple continual learning methods, such as memory-based, regularization-based methods?

* Although previous data is not available, it is able to distill data from the network of $f_i^{CL}$ with data free knowledge distillation method, as the baseline Model-inverse-ED. It is unclear to me why the proposed method is better than model-inversion. For example, if the distilled data is very close to original raw data and stores it in a memory buffer, it should have competitive performance. 

* It is unclear why the proposed methods need to perform matching in the latent space, i.e., why the methods in Section 3.1 and 3.2 are not sufficient to address the problem. 

* It seems that the proposed methods are also applicable to general data-free continual learning. Thus, the connection of the proposed methods with multi agent continual learning is weak.

The paper is clearly written, but needs to be further improved as the above comments.

The proposed methods seem reproducible.

content.title: Answer to the reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will surely take these into account in preparing an improved version. Below, we shortly answer the reviewer's individual comments.

> The proposed methods have limited novelty, the method simply combines two kinds of knowledge distillation in the model output and in latent space. Also, adopt some methods by sampling data from external resources, which are common procedures in existing works.

As far as we know, we are the first to do double distillation on the latent space (PLD). The other components have been used in some form but their combination is both novel and effective. This is also confirmed by the strong results we obtain in the experiments. Therefore, we believe it’s still an important contribution.

> What is the memory cost for the proposed methods, especially compared to traditional and simple continual learning methods, such as memory-based, regularization-based methods?

The adaptation is a simple naive finetuning, faster than replay and regularization methods. The consolidation is a double knowledge distillation, so it requires three forward passes, while LwF requires two.

> Although previous data is not available, it is able to distill data from the network of with data free knowledge distillation method, as the baseline Model-inverse-ED

In general, model inversion methods do not work in this setting. The main problem seems to be the diversity of the data, which is very limited with model inversion. We show some results in Table 1.b. We also did some preliminary experiments with model inversion without success.
You can find additional results with model inversion in [1], which are consistent with our view.

[1] Carta, Antonio, et al. "Ex-Model: Continual Learning from a Stream of Trained Models." _Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition_. 2022.

> For example, if the distilled data is very close to original raw data and stores it in a memory buffer, it should have competitive performance.

In theory this is correct, but in practice the distilled data is never close enough to the original data to be useful. At least not in the settings we have experimented with.
	
> It is unclear why the proposed methods need to perform matching in the latent space, i.e., why the methods in Section 3.1 and 3.2 are not sufficient to address the problem.

Figure 4 provide a comparison between DAC with and without PLD. We find PLD to be beneficial to forward transfer.
	
> It seems that the proposed methods are also applicable to general data-free continual learning. Thus, the connection of the proposed methods with multi agent continual learning is weak.

The method is applicable to data-free CL since it is designed for a more restricted setting. The difference is that in our setting  the model does not have access to the current data during the consolidation, while in data-free CL the past data is unavailable but the current data can be used.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a setting called “multi-agent continual learning”. In its essence it is having multiple experts each trained on one task but initialized from its predecessor. They transfer their learned knowledge to a centralized copy using the technique of knowledge distillation, as well as distillation in the latent space using a projector. The proposed method compares favorably against other continual learning baselines without data replay.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Reasonable results: The results seem to perform favorably against other methods that do not employ data replay.

- Comparison between sequential and independent init is a good experiment to report. Figure 4b and 4c seems to suggest that the proposed DAC does better than independent and sequential w/o latent distillation, but the benefit is only significant on linear probing, which is an odd experimental setup in this context. Plus, figure 4a is not really obvious. Why not show a table with final numbers of all four variants?

- Projected latent distillation is a novel idea. However, it could be directly compared with regular knowledge distillation without the multi-agent setup. 

Weaknesses:
- Lack of a realistic setting: The paper introduces a new setting with many less well defined assumptions. See my detailed comments in the next section. It’s unclear what the authors meant by resource and privacy constraints and they seem less rigorously defined. It’s also unclear what realistic application the authors are tailoring their assumptions towards. It is a bit confusing to understand based on a first read.

- OOD data: The OOD setting also seems a bit unnecessary and less helpful anyways. See my detailed comments in the next section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Problem definition: The paper illustrates a very confusing problem setup.
Last paragraph page 2, “different stream” - how different? Why is this setup realistic?
Second paragraph page 3, “consolidates the knowledge of both models” - what are “both models”?
Second paragraph page 3 “We will use an out-of-distribution dataset” - where is the ood dataset coming from? How ood is it going to be?
There are so many loose ends in the definition which makes it hardly a problem definition, nor is it connected to real applications in any way.

- Problem assumptions: First paragraph of section 2: “However, due to resource and privacy constraints, we assume that at time i we do not have access to data from previous experiences.” Resource constraints: please state clearly what is the resource constraint. How many bits of data are you allowed to transmit? With the bits limit, I am sure you can send some of the previous data over. Privacy constraints: It is not clear that sending the model parameters gives you any better privacy guarantees, if any at all. In fact, the literature of model inversion attacks studies exactly this problem.
Fredrikson et al. Model inversion attacks that exploit confidence information and basic countermeasures. CCS 2015. 

- Relation with Federated Continual Learning: Third paragraph page 3 introduced a federated learning scenario with a server (consolidated model) and several clients (experts). But a relevant ICML 2021 paper (arXiv available since Mar 2020) on federated continual learning is not cited or discussed. Yoon et al. Federated Continual Learning with Weighted Inter-client Transfer. ICML 2021. In the second paragraph of introduction, the author claims that “it is not possible to integrate using popular federated learning methods or to allow each agent to train independently.” This seems like a bold statement and probably requires a separate paragraph to justify. Table 3 claims that there is low synchronization overhead in the proposed paradigm but didn’t give a concrete number what is meant by “low” overhead, and what is the relation between overhead and performance.

- Claims on “multi-agent learning”: I suspect multi-agent learning is the right terminology for this paper since I only see the interaction between a task expert and a consolidated model. I don’t think “multi-agent continual learning” is an accurate characterization of the problem setup. The problem structure seems too restricted compared to a general multi-agent learning paradigm where the number of agents and the communication graph between them can vary.

- Using random data: Section 3.2: “Using random vectors would be highly inefficient.” - It would be better to explicitly point the readers to Table 2 for empirical evidence.

- Novelty: The only novelty of the paper seems to be projected latent distillation, which is mentioned on a small paragraph in page 5.

- OOD data: In Table 2, using current data is almost as good as you can get. ImageNet is slightly better (with overlaps of confidence intervals), at the cost of storing a big dataset on its own. So I don’t really understand why bringing up the issue of OOD data anyways? OOD helps very little, if any, meanwhile making the setup very confusing. It was unclear to me where the OOD data even came from. And if you chose the wrong OOD data (e.g. hubble or noise), you could also get screwed badly. Also why does “city” get chosen to appear in the final table? Why not an average of all OOD or just display in-distribution? Having OOD also makes the comparison a little unfair to other methods that do not have access to OOD.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the paper proposes latent distillation technique and showing some favorable results, but the problem setup is convoluted and not really realistic. The assumptions also seem less well justified. The focus of the paper is diluted by the OOD data. The clarity of writing needs improvement. Therefore, I am inclined towards rejection of the paper.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Answer to the reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will surely take these into account in preparing an improved version. Below, we shortly answer the reviewer's individual comments.

> the benefit is only significant on linear probing, which is an odd experimental setup in this context. Plus, figure 4a is not really obvious. Why not show a table with final numbers of all four variants?

We use the linear probing to measure whether the latent representation of the model is improving over time. Using linear probing instead of the expert’s accuracy allows to test the latent representation on unseen data (Fig. 4c) and ignore forgetting in the classifier. We agree that adding the final accuracy is helpful and we will do it in the updated paper.

> It’s unclear what the authors meant by resource and privacy constraints and they seem less rigorously defined. 

Resource and privacy constraints are popular (and often implicit) constraints in continual learning. We did not think it necessary to discuss them further since they are common assumptions in CL.

> OOD data: The OOD setting also seems a bit unnecessary and less helpful anyways.

The use of OOD data is needed because of privacy, which does not allow to use the real data during the consolidation phase.

> where is the ood dataset coming from? How ood is it going to be?

This is application-specific and we show the results of using different datasets in Table 2.

> Resource constraints: please state clearly what is the resource constraint. How many bits of data are you allowed to transmit? With the bits limit, I am sure you can send some of the previous data over.  

We assume that the expert will send the model’s parameters only once after completing the training on a single task. Raw data cannot be sent due to privacy constraints.

> Privacy constraints: It is not clear that sending the model parameters gives you any better privacy guarantees, if any at all. In fact, the literature of model inversion attacks studies exactly this problem. Fredrikson et al. Model inversion attacks that exploit confidence information and basic countermeasures. CCS 2015.

This is correct. We ignore model inversion attack since it is possible to use differential privacy methods or similar methods that are completely orthogonal from the continual learning problem which we study in this paper.

> Relation with Federated Continual Learning: Third paragraph page 3 introduced a federated learning scenario with a server (consolidated model) and several clients (experts). But a relevant ICML 2021 paper (arXiv available since Mar 2020) on federated continual learning is not cited or discussed. Yoon et al. Federated Continual Learning with Weighted Inter-client Transfer. ICML 2021.

In our setting, the model is sent only once at the end of training. Federated learning methods require frequent communication, and do not work in this setting. In fact, Table 1.b shows that averaging the model’s parameters, like many federated learning methods do, results in a low accuracy (2%, which is the same as the random baseline).

> I don’t think “multi-agent continual learning” is an accurate characterization of the problem setup. The problem structure seems too restricted compared to a general multi-agent learning paradigm where the number of agents and the communication graph between them can vary.

This is correct. We decided to focus the paper on a single aspect of the multi-agent communication, that is consolidation, which is a core problem that needs to be solved before tackling complex communication patterns.

> Using random data: Section 3.2: “Using random vectors would be highly inefficient.” - It would be better to explicitly point the readers to Table 2 for empirical evidence.

We will add the reference.
  
> Novelty: The only novelty of the paper seems to be projected latent distillation, which is mentioned on a small paragraph in page 5.

The scenario and its analysis are also novel. Regarding the methodology, while many of DAC components have been used in similar forms, there are differences with the literature and their integration is also novel.
This is also proved by the better accuracy in the experimental results.

> OOD data: In Table 2, using current data is almost as good as you can get. ImageNet is slightly better (with overlaps of confidence intervals), at the cost of storing a big dataset on its own. So I don’t really understand why bringing up the issue of OOD data anyways?

OOD data is needed because we don’t have access to the original data. Given this constraint, we provide a method that can work even with limited OOD data (single image).

> Having OOD also makes the comparison a little unfair to other methods that do not have access to OOD.

Actually, it’s the opposite. Our method is more constrained because it cannot access the original data, unlike all the other.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors propose an approach to share knowledge among distributed continual
learning agents. The key idea is to split the learning problem into an adaption and a consolidation
phase. The main contribution is a novel method to perform double knowledge distillation from out of
distribution data, which is evaluated on a set of benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
Good motivation of the problem setup. 
The authors did a great job motivating the underlying problem that needs to be solved.
Good explanation of their approach: The main idea and contribution is well explained and visualized

Room for improvements
Naming: The authors call their approach to be a "multi-agent" learning problem. Since we do not
really have any form of collaboration/competition, nor a sequential decision making problem, I
would suggest to refer to this setting as "distributed continual learning".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is well written and mostly clear.
Quality: The formal quality seems to be correct and the experimental evaluation seems to be
convincing.
Novelty: I am not familiar enough with continual learning to judge the novelty of this approach.
Reproducibility: The authors provide the code to reproduce the results of their project along with the
necessary dependencies. However, it would have been nice to include a small set of instructions to
start some of the experiments. The readme file does not include any hint how to run them.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe that the presented approach is a good contribution to the outlined problem description. The
authors motivated the application domain well and clearly explained the proposed algorithm. Since I do
not have a background in continual learning, I can not make any statement on the novelty for this
paper. Moreover, although the experimental evaluation seems to be convincing, due to my lack of
experience in this area I might not be able to clearly put the numbers in context.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.title: Answer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will surely take these into account in preparing an improved version. Below, we shortly answer the reviewer's individual comments.

> Naming: The authors call their approach to be a "multi-agent" learning problem. Since we do not really have any form of collaboration/competition, nor a sequential decision making problem, I would suggest to refer to this setting as "distributed continual learning".

The objective of the paper was to describe a novel scenario (multi-agent CL) and focus on the core problem of such scenario (consolidation) without caring too much about other aspects, to limit the complexity of the work and its presentation. However, the result of this choice is that we don’t have any complex interaction between agents. We will consider substituting the “multi-agent CL” scenario with a more restricted setting to improve the readability of the paper in the future version.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method of using ensemble of experts model with a novel consolidation method (a double knowledge distillation scheme, named Data-Agnostic Consolidation) via a new loss called Projected Latent Distillation (PLD). The proposed method is evaluated on SplitCIFAR100 and CORe50 dataset, outperforming some prior arts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- S1: The first ensemble approach in continual learning that outperforms some of the representative CL methods in SplitCIFAR100 dataset.
- S2: The proposed KD loss configuration is novel for mixing the output of ensemble models.

**Weaknesses**
- W1: **There is no ablation study to investigate the benefit of each proposed component** -- it is not clear that how much each proposed components (e.g., a - ensembling, b - PLD) contribute to the performance. Specifically, it is necessary to comparing the performance of the proposed method with the same sized single model (a model that combines the previous model and new expert model) instead of having multiple experts for fair performance comparison. The proposed PLD loss looks trivial and its benefit is not clear.
- W2: **Compared methods are quite old** -- as the compared methods are from a survey paper published in 2020, the compared methods are quite outdated. There are numerous advances in continual learning, especially the rehearsal based method. It is recommended to compare the proposed method with them. To name a few of rehearsal based methods,
  - Wang et al., "Continual Learning with Lifelong Vision Transformer", CVPR 2022
  - Hersche et al., "Constrained Few-shot Class-incremental Learning", CVPR 2022
  - Wan et al., "Continual Learning for Visual Search with Backward Consistent Feature Embedding", CVPR 2022
  - Tang et al., "Learning to Imagine: Diversify Memory for Incremental Learning using Unlabeled Data", CVPR 2022
  - Bang et al., "Rainbow memory: Continual learning with a memory of diverse samples", CVPR 2021
- W3: **Empirical results are weak** -- Given that the paper's proposal is quite heuristic, the empirical validation is of importance. However, the paper adopts only two datasets for the empirical validation (whereas many empirical/heuristic papers in the literature adopts 3-4 datasets for their validations) and even one of them is in small scale -- SplitCIFAR100. Thus, the empirical validation is not that strong.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- **Clarity**: The paper is pretty clearly presented. 
- **Quality**: Quality of the paper is reasonable but not sufficient as a compelling proposal.
- **Novelty**: It has some novel aspects in the proposed method but not very interesting to general audience of continual learning researchers in the reviewer's opinion.
- **Reproducibility**: The method is quite simple thus could be well reproducible. But there is no open source repository of this proposal.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given that the method is quite heuristic and empirical validation does not well support the benefit of the proposal, it is not sufficient to be reported to the community yet. Rather, revising the method with stronger empirical results will increase the value of the submission in the future venues.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: Answer to the reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We will surely take these into account in preparing an improved version. Below, we shortly answer the reviewer's individual comments.

> W1: **There is no ablation study to investigate the benefit of each proposed component** -- it is not clear that how much each proposed components (e.g., a - ensembling, b - PLD)

We would like to point out that the proposed method is not an ensemble of models. The result of DAC is a single model. The only ensemble methods in the paper are the baselines in the first 4 rows of Table 2.b.
In Table 1.a we have a model that performs single KD (LwF) and double KD with OOD data (DMC).
Finally, In the Section “COMPARISON BETWEEN SEQUENTIAL AND INDEPENDENT SCENARIO”, we have a comparison between DAC with and without PLD in different settings.

> W2: **Compared methods are quite old** -- as the compared methods are from a survey paper published in 2020, the compared methods are quite outdated. There are numerous advances in continual learning, especially the rehearsal based method. It is recommended to compare the proposed method with them. 

The paper focuses on rehearsal-free and task-aware settings. Unfortunately, the papers suggested by the reviewer are all rehearsal method and/or class-incremental methods, which are not applicable to the scenario studied in this paper.

>  W3: **Empirical results are weak** -- Given that the paper's proposal is quite heuristic, the empirical validation is of importance. However, the paper adopts only two datasets for the empirical validation (whereas many empirical/heuristic papers in the literature adopts 3-4 datasets for their validations) and even one of them is in small scale -- SplitCIFAR100. Thus, the empirical validation is not that strong.

We will add another dataset to extend the experimental analysis.

> **Reproducibility**: The method is quite simple thus could be well reproducible. But there is no open source repository of this proposal.

We provided the source code as supplementary material.
